lines.text: $x = \hl{1}{2}$ is point $A$, so $B$ and $C$ have $x = \hl{1}{4.5}$ and $x = \hl{1}{7}$ (B is left of C on the graph). Their $y$-coordinate is $0$.

problems.note: The root x = -1 is given, and the quadratic factor 2x² - 23x + 63 is the same as in the last problem. This time you find it by long division by (x + 1) instead of grouping. The slots keep the same meanings.

steps.ask: What must you multiply x + 1 by so that its leading term matches 2x³?
steps.title: Divide f(x) by (x + 1): first term

lines.text: Divide the leading terms: $2x^3 \div x = 2x^2$.

steps.ask: Subtract what you have just written from f(x). What is left?
steps.title: Subtract to leave the remainder so far

steps.ask: Divide the leading term of what is left by x. What is the next term of the quotient?
steps.title: Second term of the quotient

lines.text: Divide the leading terms: $-23x^2 \div x = -23x$.

steps.ask: Subtract again, the same way. What is left?
steps.title: Subtract again

steps.ask: What is the last term of the quotient, and what is the remainder?
steps.title: Third term of the quotient

lines.text: Divide the leading terms: $63x \div x = 63$.
Subtracting leaves $0$, so the quotient is $\hl{3}{2x^2 - 23x + 63}$.

steps.ask: What two numbers multiply to 126 and add to -23?
steps.title: Factorise the quadratic

lines.text: Find two numbers with product $2 \times 63 = 126$ and sum $-23$: they are $-14$ and $-9$.

steps.title: Set f(x) = 0 and solve each factor

lines.text: $-8$ lies on the negative real axis, so $r = \hl{1}{8}$ and $\theta = \hl{2}{\pi}$.

problems.note: There are two roots this time, not three, and the number is already in polar form. The method is the same: root the modulus, halve the angle, then read off each value. The ± gives both roots instead of trying n = 0 and n = 1.

steps.ask: If w squared is v, how many values can w take?
steps.title: Take the square root of v

lines.text: $w^2 = v$ means $w = \pm v^{1/2}$.

steps.ask: What happens to the modulus and to the angle when you raise to the power one half?
steps.title: Apply De Moivre's theorem

lines.text: $\left[r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\right]^{n} = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)$. Here $n = \tfrac12$: square-root the modulus and halve the angle.
